extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent prosecution practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for supporting or rebutting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 during patent examination, including acceptable rationales, sources of rationale, and procedural limits on relying on common knowledge or legal precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable claim interpretation; no speculative interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner must not simply speculate about the meaning of claim language and then enter an obviousness rejection based on that speculative interpretation. A claim should not be rejected over prior art merely because it is indefinite; if a claim is susceptible to more than one interpretation, the examiner should not base a rejection on an interpretation that is not reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Steele, In re Wilson, Ionescu; see MPEP § 2111 regarding proper claim interpretation. If claim language is considered indefinite, do not disregard the language or treat indefiniteness as a basis to reject unless a reasonable interpretation supports the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of all claim limitations (including negatives and new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating obviousness, all limitations of the claims must be considered and given weight, including limitations that do not find support in the original specification (negative limitations or new matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All words in a claim must be considered when judging patentability against the prior art. See Ex parte Grasselli, In re Miller, and In re Wilson as authority that negative or unsupported claim limitations cannot be ignored in an obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible sources of rationale for combining references
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationale to modify or combine the prior art may be found in the prior art (express or implied), reasoned from common knowledge in the art, established scientific principles, art-recognized equivalents, or legal precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References need not explicitly teach a suggestion to combine; implicit teachings and ordinary skill in the art can supply the rationale. See In re Fine, In re Jones, In re Kotzab, In re Eli Lilly, In re Nilssen, Ex parte Clapp, Ex parte Levengood for examples and tests for implicit teachings and reliance on legal precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of some advantage as strongest rationale to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: A recognition (express or implied in the prior art, or drawn from convincing reasoning/scientific principles/legal precedent) that some advantage or expected beneficial result would be produced by combining references is the strongest rationale for combining references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages may be technology-independent (e.g., stronger, cheaper, cleaner, faster, lighter, more durable, more efficient) and support a motivation to combine even absent explicit suggestion. See In re Sernaker and Dystar Textilfarben v. C.H. Patrick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal precedent usable only when facts are sufficiently similar
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may use legal precedent as the rationale supporting an obviousness rejection only if the facts in the prior legal decision are sufficiently similar (analogizable) to those in the application so that they present the same legal issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarity need not be in the same technological area; it is sufficient that the facts can be analogized to present the same legal question. Do not rely solely on precedent if the applicant has demonstrated the criticality of a specific limitation. See KSR, In re Eli Lilly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale may differ from applicant's stated purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible for the examiner to identify a reason or motivation to modify the prior art that is different from the purpose or problem the applicant identified; motivation can arise from the general problem confronting the inventor rather than the specific problem addressed by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation to combine need not show identical problem-solving intent; see In re Kahn, Cross Med. Prods. v. Medtronic, In re Lintner, In re Dillon for examples where prior art provided motivation even if for different purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit disclosure: consider inferences a skilled artisan would draw
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing the disclosure of a reference, it is proper to consider not only the specific teachings but also the inferences that one skilled in the art would reasonably be expected to draw from the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Preda (temperature ranges implying higher temperatures), In re Lamberti (implications about R groups). Use tests for implicit teachings (see In re Kotzab).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on scientific theory requires evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner relies on a scientific theory as the rationale for a prima facie obviousness finding, the existence and meaning of that theory must be provided and supported by evidence in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have rejected obviousness findings based on unsupported scientific theory (In re Grose; zeolite/crystal-form example). Provide documentary or expert evidence when invoking technical theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official notice/common knowledge should be used judiciously; prefer citing prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may take official notice of facts or rely on common knowledge in the art only in limited circumstances; when reasonably possible the examiner should cite a prior art reference instead of relying on official notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official notice without documentary evidence is permissible only when the facts are 'capable of such instant and unquestionable demonstration as to defy dispute' (In re Ahlert, In re Knapp Monarch). It should be rarely used when an application is under final rejection or action under 37 CFR 1.113.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not take official notice of disputed or esoteric technical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inappropriate to take official notice of facts that are not beyond dispute or are esoteric; assertions of technical facts in specialized areas must be supported by reference to standard works or documentary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Ahlert, In re Grose, In re Eynde: esoteric or specialized facts require documentary support; do not claim 'state of the art' by official notice where reasonable disagreement exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never rely solely on common knowledge as the principal evidence for a rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection must not be based principally on the examiner's assertion of common knowledge in the art without evidentiary support in the record; findings of fact must be supported by substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zurko and Arendi emphasize that the Board/examiner cannot simply reach conclusions based on own understanding or 'common sense' without concrete evidence in the record. Provide documentary support when common knowledge is a primary basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: If official notice is taken, provide clear, explicit technical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When taking official notice of a fact without documentary evidence, the technical line of reasoning underlying that decision must be clear and unmistakable, with specific factual findings and sound technical/scientific reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Soli, In re Chevenard: the basis for the notice must be set forth explicitly so the applicant can adequately traverse the finding in the next reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: If applicant traverses an officially-noticed fact, examiner must support the finding with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant properly traverses an examiner's assertion of official notice or common knowledge, the examiner must provide documentary evidence or an affidavit/declaration in the next Office action to maintain the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere request from applicant for documentary evidence is not an adequate traverse; applicant must specifically point out errors. See 37 CFR 1.111(b), 37 CFR 1.104(d)(2), Chevenard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality considerations when adding references after a traverse
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner adds a reference in the next Office action solely to support a prior common-knowledge finding and it does not introduce a new issue or ground of rejection, the Office action may be made final; otherwise it should not be made final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the newly cited reference is added for other reasons or introduces a new ground of rejection, the action may not be made final. See MPEP § 706.07(a) and discussion in § 2144.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use legal precedent as a rationale only after showing applicability to the facts
rubrics_metrics.description: In formulating a rejection that invokes legal precedent, the examiner must ensure the precedent's rationale is explained and shown to apply to the facts at hand; do not rely solely on case law if applicant has demonstrated a limitation's criticality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 2144.04: provide explanation and factual connection to precedent; examples of routine expedients from case law are discussed but must be tied to application facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic/ornamental design changes often not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes that relate to ornamentation only and have no mechanical function cannot be relied upon to patentably distinguish a claimed invention from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Seid as authority; however, product shape may be significant where it results in a product distinct from the reference (see Ex parte Hilton). Evaluate function/ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if the function is not desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing an element (and thereby omitting its function) from a prior art device is obvious if the omitted function is not desired or required in the claimed context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ex parte Wu, In re Larson, In re Kuhle. If the prior art feature serves a function not needed in the claimed use, omitting it may be an obvious expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element with retention of its function is an indicium of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim omits an element of the prior art but nonetheless retains the function of that element (i.e., achieves the same function differently), this can indicate nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Edge: elimination of an element while retaining its function (via a different structure) supported nonobviousness because the function remained and the prior art approach was distinguishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automating a manual activity is not sufficient to distinguish over prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly providing an automatic or mechanical means to replace a manual activity that accomplishes the same result is generally not sufficient to render the claim nonobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Venner: automating an old manual activity (e.g., adding timer/solenoid to known structures) is typically an obvious substitution unless unexpected results are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in size or proportion (scaling) are not patentable absent different performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere scaling up (or changing proportions) of a prior art device or process that would not perform differently does not establish patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Rose, In re Rinehart, Gardner v. TEC Sys. examples: if relative dimensions/scale produce no different performance, the change is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in shape/configuration are generally obvious absent persuasive evidence of significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of a particular shape or configuration is often a matter of choice that a person of ordinary skill would find obvious, unless evidence shows the configuration has significant technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Dailey: configuration alone is insufficient absent persuasive evidence that the shape yields a novel functional result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in sequence of process steps are prima facie obvious absent unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of any order of performing process steps or mixing ingredients is prima facie obvious in the absence of new or unexpected results from the changed sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Rubin, In re Burhans, In re Gibson: reversing or changing order of known process steps is prima facie obvious unless the new sequence yields unexpected benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a device portable, integral, separable, adjustable, or continuous is often routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifying a known device to be portable, integral, separable, adjustable, or to operate continuously is typically within ordinary engineering choice and may be obvious unless it achieves new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sub-examples: making portable (In re Lindberg) not sufficient alone; making integral often obvious (In re Larson) unless it eliminates a known problem (Schenck v. Nortron); making separable obvious if desirable (In re Dulberg); making adjustable not patentable if adjustment is a known need (In re Stevens); making continuous versus batch may be obvious (In re Dilnot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal, duplication, or rearrangement of parts is commonly prima facie obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing, duplicating, or rearranging parts of a known device is generally an obvious modification unless such changes produce new and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reversal of parts (In re Gazda), duplication without new result (In re Harza), and rearrangement are treated as prima facie obvious in the absence of an unexpected technical effect.
